{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts frequently use specific titles (Dr., Mag., Prof., etc.) and role markers (Richter, Richterin, Beschwerdeführer) to identify persons. The main challenge is distinguishing between person names and other capitalized nouns or company names, which requires anchoring to these specific titles or roles rather than just capitalization.",
  "strategy": "Create a set of focused regex rules that anchor person names to preceding titles (Dr., Mag., etc.) or specific role phrases (Richter, Richterin, Beschwerdeführer), ensuring high precision by requiring these context anchors.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use Unicode support for German characters (ä, ö, ü, ß).",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "Judge_Richter",
      "description": "Captures person names following 'Richter' or 'Richterin' (with optional titles like Mag., Dr., Prof.).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:die|der|durch\\s+)?(?:Richterin|Richter)(?:\\s+(?:Mag\\.?|Dr\\.?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Bakk\\.?)?\\s+)?([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "High frequency in legal texts; anchors to the role 'Richter/Richterin' which is a strong context indicator for a person."
    },
    {
      "name": "Representative_Dr_Mag",
      "description": "Captures person names following 'vertreten durch' (represented by) or 'durch' (by) with titles like Dr., Mag., etc.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:vertreten\\s+durch|durch)\\s+([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+(?:Dr\\.?|Mag\\.?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Bakk\\.?)?\\s+)?[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Common pattern for legal representatives; the phrase 'vertreten durch' is a strong anchor."
    },
    {
      "name": "Complainant_Beschwerdeführer",
      "description": "Captures person names following 'Beschwerdesache' (complaint case) or 'Beschwerdeführer' (complainant).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:in\\s+der\\s+Beschwerdesache|Beschwerdeführer(?:in)?(?:,|:)?)\\s+([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Anchors to the legal context of a complaint case or the explicit role of complainant."
    },
    {
      "name": "Title_Dr_Mag_Prefix",
      "description": "Captures person names starting with titles like Dr., Mag., Prof. at the beginning of a sentence or after punctuation.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:^|[,;:]\\s+)(Dr\\.?|Mag\\.?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Bakk\\.?)\\s+([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$2",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Catches names that start with a title but might not have a preceding role marker like 'Richter'. Uses capture group $2 to exclude the title from the output text if desired, but here we capture the full name part after the title."
    },
    {
      "name": "Herr_Frau_Prefix",
      "description": "Captures person names following 'Herr' or 'Frau' (Mr./Mrs.).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Herr|Frau)\\s+([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "'Herr' and 'Frau' are common honorifics in German legal texts that strongly indicate a person's name follows."
    },
    {
      "name": "Initial_Moniker",
      "description": "Captures single letter monikers like 'M.' when used as a person reference in context (e.g., 'Herr M.', 'an Herrn M.').",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Herrn?|an\\s+)?([A-Z]\\.)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "Handles anonymized references like 'M.' which appear frequently in the training data as person entities."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

      "content": "(?:vertreten\\s+durch|durch)\\s+([A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+(?:Dr\\.?|Mag\\.?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Bakk\\.?)?\\s+)?[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zäöüÄÖÜß]+)*)"

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:

- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.
